title: Arrays and Vectors
relevance: Interviewers use arrays vs vectors to check whether candidates understand fixed vs dynamic storage, stack vs heap placement, and safe default choices in C++.

phases.goal: Establish that arrays are fixed-size and vectors are dynamic, and where each lives in memory.

must_hit.point: An array is a fixed-size block of memory; a vector is a dynamic, resizable array that can grow or shrink at runtime.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States fixed versus growable as the core distinction between array and vector.

must_hit.point: Arrays usually live on the stack; std::vector always stores its elements on the heap.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts stack for arrays with heap for vector element storage.

must_hit.point: Array size must be known at compile time; vector size is determined at runtime.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Ties compile-time sizing to arrays and runtime sizing to vectors.

probes: What is the fundamental difference between a C++ array and a std::vector, and where does each live in memory?

hints.1: Think about whether the size can change after creation.
hints.2: Fixed size lets the compiler place storage on the stack; unknown growth forces heap allocation.
hints.3: Array: fixed size, usually stack, size at compile time. Vector: resizable, always heap, size at runtime.

phases.goal: Explain how vector growth works via capacity and reallocation, and why raw arrays are risky.

must_hit.point: A vector holds a fixed capacity; when insertion would exceed it, it allocates a larger heap block (typically double the current size), copies existing elements, and releases the old block.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes capacity, reallocation steps, and typically doubling.

must_hit.point: Because capacity doubles when exhausted, reallocations occur exponentially less often as the vector grows, so amortized insertion cost stays small.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Links doubling growth to rare reallocations and small average cost.

must_hit.point: Prefer std::array over raw C-style arrays: same performance, plus bounds checking and other safety features.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names std::array as the safer fixed-size alternative to int arr[].

probes: What happens internally when a std::vector runs out of capacity on push_back?

hints.1: It does not grow by a single element each time.
hints.2: Walk through allocate-new-block, copy, free-old-block, and how much larger the new block typically is.
hints.3: Typically doubles capacity, copies all elements to the new heap block, then releases the old one; doubling keeps amortized cost low.

phases.goal: Compare rigidity/speed/memory exactness of arrays against flexibility and resizing overhead of vectors.

must_hit.point: Arrays are extremely fast with zero overhead and use exactly the memory they need; vectors are still fast but pay slight resizing overhead and over-allocate for growth.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Pairs zero-overhead exact sizing for arrays with slight overhead and over-allocation for vectors.

must_hit.point: The array-versus-vector choice is flexibility versus rigidity: fixed stack-friendly storage versus growable heap storage.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Frames the decision as fixed/rigid versus dynamic/flexible.

probes: When would you accept a vector's over-allocation instead of an array's exact memory use?

hints.1: Compare what each optimizes for: speed and exact size versus room to grow.
hints.2: Mention zero overhead and exact fit for arrays versus slight resize cost and spare capacity for vectors.
hints.3: Prefer vector when size may change; accept over-allocation because amortized growth cost stays small and out-of-bounds risk drops.

phases.goal: State the practical default: use std::vector unless the size is truly known in advance.

must_hit.point: Default to std::vector for almost everything; heap allocation cost is negligible for most programs and flexibility removes a class of out-of-bounds errors.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says vector is the default and cites negligible cost plus fewer OOB mistakes.

must_hit.point: Reach for std::array only when the element count is genuinely known in advance, such as holding the three coordinates of a point.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives a fixed-size example like three point coordinates for std::array.

probes: In new C++ code, when do you choose std::vector versus std::array?

hints.1: Ask whether the count is known before the program runs.
hints.2: Default one way; reserve the fixed wrapper for truly compile-time sizes.
hints.3: Default to std::vector; use std::array only for known-ahead sizes like three coordinates of a point.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Arrays are fixed-size, usually stack-resident, compile-time sized, zero-overhead, and memory-exact; vectors are runtime-sized, always heap-backed, slightly slower due to resizing, and over-allocate so they can grow.

Default to std::vector for flexibility and fewer out-of-bounds errors; use std::array only when the size is genuinely known in advance and a fixed stack-resident block is enough and maximally efficient.
Prefer std::array over raw int arr[]: same performance as a fixed array, with bounds checking and other safety features.

gotchas.trap: Declaring an array for ten items and later needing an eleventh has no recourse—writing past the end overflows the array's storage.
gotchas.correction: Array size is locked at creation; use a growable container like std::vector when the count may increase, or size the fixed storage correctly up front.

gotchas.trap: Assuming a vector grows by one element at a time on each insertion.
gotchas.correction: It keeps a capacity and only reallocates when full: typically allocates a doubled heap block, copies elements over, and frees the old block.

gotchas.trap: Reaching for raw C-style arrays by default for fixed sequences.
gotchas.correction: Prefer std::array for fixed sizes (same performance, more safety) and std::vector when the size is not known in advance.
